title: Canonical Python module is `dontpanic_orchestrate`; `jarvis_orchestrate` becomes a non-removing compatibility shim
body:
Direction: implementation lives at `scripts/dontpanic_orchestrate/`. The legacy package at `scripts/jarvis_orchestrate/` becomes a thin shim that re-exports from the canonical module and emits a one-shot `DeprecationWarning` per process. The shim is non-removing in v1 — there is no deletion date, only a deprecation signal. Future removal is a separate plan with its own timeline.

Reason: after plan 2026-05-03-003 the brand renamed to DontPanic. The Python module direction should match. Leaving the canonical name as `jarvis_orchestrate` means every subsequent slice that touches imports is anchored on the legacy name; rename gets either dragged along or rebased against. Flipping once now is cheaper than flipping incrementally.

How to apply: `dontpanic_orchestrate` contains every business-logic module. `jarvis_orchestrate` contains only the shim plumbing — `__init__.py` plus per-submodule re-export files. The shim does NOT contain implementation. A grep assertion (acceptance #5) verifies the canonical tree has zero `jarvis_orchestrate` references; a second grep (acceptance #6) verifies the shim contains no business logic.

title: Shim shape — explicit per-submodule re-export modules + lazy `__getattr__` proxy + one-shot DeprecationWarning
body:
The compatibility shim uses three layers:

(1) `scripts/jarvis_orchestrate/__init__.py` re-exports the canonical package's module-level surface (`__version__`, any top-level public symbols) and triggers the deprecation guard.

(2) For every public submodule X (cli, supervisor, plan_loader, agent_manifest, mcp_server, projects_registry, project_config, global_config, gate_pause, inbox, audit_writer, signoff_writer, circuit_breakers, etc.), an explicit module file `scripts/jarvis_orchestrate/X.py` exists containing exactly: a one-line deprecation-guard import (no-op after first call) and `from dontpanic_orchestrate.X import *`. Explicit modules cover the common `from jarvis_orchestrate.X import Y` pattern AND the `import jarvis_orchestrate.X as Z` pattern.

(3) A package-level `__getattr__` in `scripts/jarvis_orchestrate/__init__.py` lazily proxies any attribute not enumerated, covering submodule access patterns we missed and any future submodule added to the canonical tree without a corresponding shim file.

(4) The deprecation guard emits exactly one `DeprecationWarning` per process via a module-level `_warned: bool` flag. The warning message names the canonical replacement and points at this plan as authority.

Reason for explicit per-submodule files (not just `__getattr__`): some Python tooling (mypy, IDE auto-import, `python -m jarvis_orchestrate.cli`) relies on filesystem-based module discovery. Explicit files make the legacy path discoverable to those tools while keeping zero business logic in the shim.

How to apply: F001 step 5. The shim test file (step 9) verifies all public submodules import successfully via the legacy name and that the deprecation warning fires exactly once per process under `pytest.warns(DeprecationWarning)`.

title: Historical plan dirs, evidence strings, and audit envelopes are durable records — NOT renamed
body:
Operator-supplied tightening at draft time. The rename touches *live* import surfaces and *canonical* operator-facing docs. It does NOT rewrite audit history.

Not touched by this plan:
- `docs/plans/2026-04-XX-001-jarvis-...` slugs (durable plan IDs per `feedback_plan_id_brand_policy` memory)
- Historical file contents under `docs/plans/` outside this plan's own new directory — evidence files, decisions.jsonl entries, audit envelope JSON, signoff JSON, transcripts, INBOX.md (where present)
- Memory entries under `~/.claude/projects/.../memory/*.md` that reference Jarvis as a brand-historic name
- The agent-conventions subtree at `claude/shared/` (upstream — touching it requires a coordinated convention version bump, separate plan)

Reason: the rename is about live import surfaces. Audit history and historical plan metadata are durable records — rewriting them would conflate brand-rename motion with rewriting evidence of what shipped under the old brand. The plan-id brand policy memory already pins this principle. This plan's own directory is new current-plan evidence and is allowed by the commit boundary.

How to apply: `protected_paths` lists `docs/plans/` and `claude/shared/`. The acceptance test (#10) asserts `git diff --name-only HEAD` for this commit shows zero entries under historical `docs/plans/` directories outside this plan's own new directory. A grep step is acceptable for `claude/shared/` if `protected_paths` enforcement is not directly tooled.

title: Console-script direction decoupled from internal module direction — both `dontpanic` and `jarvis` resolve to the canonical entrypoint
body:
User-facing console scripts and internal Python module direction are decoupled. After this refactor:

- `dontpanic` console script → `dontpanic_orchestrate.cli:main` (canonical)
- `jarvis` console script → `dontpanic_orchestrate.cli:main` (legacy alias, same target)

Both scripts invoke the canonical entrypoint directly. There is no behavioral difference between the two; the `jarvis` name stays as a legacy alias for users who still type it from muscle memory. The legacy console script is non-removing in v1 — its removal is a separate plan with its own timeline.

Reason: console-script naming and internal module naming are different surfaces with different removal economics. A user typing `jarvis dispatch-from-plan` should not break because the internal module renamed. The console-script alias is cheap to keep; the import alias is what carries cost (deprecation warnings, double-discovery in tooling) and is the surface this plan is about flipping.

How to apply: `pyproject.toml` `[project.scripts]` block has both keys mapping to `dontpanic_orchestrate.cli:main`. Acceptance #3 verifies both `which dontpanic` and `which jarvis` resolve to the canonical entrypoint by reading the resolved console-script shim.

title: Direct-path execution; no volley
body:
Plan A executes via direct path. The auditor would have nothing semantic to debate — the rename is mechanical and the acceptance is deterministic (every test green pre-rename must be green post-rename, plus explicit grep assertions).

Reason: volley quota is finite (~13% of weekly cap per round). The queued slices that follow this plan (Plan B = lifecycle-staged gates; Plan C = subprocess timeout / envelope durability) are real semantic changes that benefit from adversarial review. Spending volley quota on a rename refactor would be misallocation.

How to apply: `loop_caps.max_iterations: 1` in plan.md frontmatter. No `audit/` envelope generation expected (the directory is created for plan-validator compliance only). Close-out goes through direct review on the operator's machine, mirroring the F001-of-plan-003 close-out pattern.

title: Shim removal is a separately-planned future slice with its own deprecation timeline
body:
The `jarvis_orchestrate` shim and the `jarvis` console-script alias are both non-removing in this refactor. Removal is explicitly out of scope.

Reason: removal needs a deprecation cycle the ecosystem can observe — at minimum, one or more releases that emit the `DeprecationWarning` at WARNING level so downstream consumers (other repos that imported `jarvis_orchestrate`, or scripts that ran `jarvis ...`) have time to migrate. Bundling removal into the rename slice would fail consumers who have already pinned the legacy name.

How to apply: this plan's acceptance does not include shim deletion. A future plan (suggested ID: `YYYY-MM-DD-NNN-refactor-remove-jarvis-orchestrate-shim`) would add: (a) bump warning category to a louder visibility level, (b) audit downstream consumers, (c) drop the shim files + console-script alias + packaging exclusions, (d) close out. That plan is NOT drafted here — wait for migration evidence before scheduling.

title: Plan locked with no-shim-relay tightening — AC #11 added before flip to active
body:
Operator reviewed the draft and locked it with one acceptance addition: AC #11 verifies that canonical surfaces (`python -m dontpanic_orchestrate ...`, `dontpanic` console script, direct `dontpanic_orchestrate.cli.main(...)` calls) emit ZERO `DeprecationWarning` from `jarvis_orchestrate`. The deprecation signal fires ONLY when consumers explicitly import the legacy name (AC #2).

Reason: catches the subtle failure mode where the rename looks complete from a tree-survey perspective (canonical files exist, shim files exist, tests pass) but the new package still routes internal calls through the legacy module — for example, if `dontpanic_orchestrate.cli.main` happens to import `jarvis_orchestrate.supervisor` somewhere in its dependency graph. AC #5 (grep-based) catches this for source files; AC #11 catches it at runtime via the deprecation-warning channel, which is the strongest assertion that canonical execution is fully self-contained.

Also tightened: AC #5 explicitly allows `tests/test_legacy_shim_compatibility.py` to import the legacy name (the shim is the unit under test in that file). All other files in the canonical tree must be self-referential.

Lock authority: operator (this turn). Plan flipped `status: draft` → `status: active` after these edits land. Implementation may begin.

How to apply: see AC #11 + step 9(f) in F001. The runtime no-shim-relay test wraps two representative CLI subcommand invocations (`manifest show --json`, `projects list --json`) in `warnings.catch_warnings()` with `simplefilter('error', DeprecationWarning)`.
